package_info.why_malicious: This package is part of a large-scale campaign (over 140,000 packages) designed to lure users into phishing scams by embedding links to credential-harvesting and referral-reward phishing sites directly in the package description. The packages are auto-generated, use enticing names related to free codes or cheats, and are published en masse to poison the ecosystem, increase search visibility, and drive traffic to malicious sites.

execution_context.trigger: When the package metadata is parsed (during install-time, search-time, or view-time in the NuGet ecosystem)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: When the package metadata is displayed (install-time, search-time, or view-time), the description field presents enticing text and embedded phishing URLs; this exposes users to external phishing sites by encouraging them to click the links, resulting in redirection to credential-harvesting or scam pages.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The description embeds phishing URLs and uses manipulative language to entice users into clicking, which is a clear abuse of package metadata for malicious purposes. The intent is to redirect users to external phishing or scam sites, not to inform about the package.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate package descriptions provide technical or usage information about the software and may link only to official documentation or project homepages. They do not contain unrelated, reward-based, or credential-harvesting links, nor do they attempt to lure users with promises of free codes or cheats.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may include links to official documentation or project websites, but never to unrelated, reward-based, or phishing domains. Any external links should be directly relevant to the package and not designed to entice or mislead.
key_indicators: Description field contains multiple external URLs unrelated to the project
Use of enticing language promising free codes, cheats, or rewards
Presence of known phishing or scam domains (e.g., gamecodeclaim.com)
No actual software functionality—package exists solely for SEO/phishing
Auto-generated or mass-published package names referencing hacks, cheats, or free codes

attack_chain.action: Automated creation and publication of large numbers of packages with enticing names and phishing links embedded in the description field.
attack_chain.leads_to: Users searching for packages encounter the phishing links in search results or package listings.

attack_chain.action: User views or installs the package and sees the description, which promises free codes, cheats, or rewards and contains embedded phishing URLs.
attack_chain.leads_to: User is enticed to click the phishing link.

attack_chain.action: User clicks the phishing link and is redirected to an external phishing site, which may simulate a reward process and then request sensitive information or redirect to further scam or referral sites.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credential harvesting, survey fraud, or abuse of referral reward programs.

behavioral_signatures: Package descriptions containing multiple external URLs unrelated to the project or documentation
Descriptions using language that promises free codes, cheats, followers, or rewards
Mass publication of similarly structured packages with auto-generated, enticing names
Descriptions referencing known phishing or scam domains (e.g., gamecodeclaim.com, tinybit.cc, gamecoins.codes)
Packages with no actual code or functionality, only SEO/phishing content in metadata
file_indicators: nuspec files with description fields containing suspicious or unrelated URLs
Package names referencing hacks, cheats, free codes, followers, or similar lures
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests or user redirections to domains such as gamecodeclaim.com, tinybit.cc, gamecoins.codes, and other known phishing IOCs
Redirections to eCommerce or survey sites with suspicious referral or affiliate parameters (e.g., AliExpress with ?af=... parameter)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Automated scanners should parse package metadata, especially the description field, to identify external URLs. Flag packages where URLs match known phishing or scam domains, or where the description uses language promising free rewards, cheats, or codes. Monitor for mass publication patterns and auto-generated package names. Correlate with IOC domain lists. Alert on packages lacking legitimate code or functionality but containing SEO/phishing content in metadata.
